stem: This question is about the agents of socialisation.

parts.label: (a)

payload.template: A person, group or institution that teaches an individual how to behave in society is an {{blank:a}} of socialisation. Learning in early childhood within the family is called {{blank:b}} socialisation.

parts.explanation: An agent of socialisation teaches behaviour; primary socialisation happens first, in the family.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Match each agent of socialisation with what it **mainly** teaches.

right.content: Moral teachings, worship and rites of passage
Punctuality, discipline and respect for rules
Shared interests, group norms and fashions

parts.explanation: School: rules and routines. Peers: group norms. Religious groups: moral teaching and worship.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how the community socialises young people.

points.description: Elders and neighbours guide, correct and advise children, so good behaviour is expected everywhere, not only at home
Work parties (nhimbe / ilima) and community projects teach cooperation and hard work, because young people work alongside adults
Any one further point: ceremonies teach customs and roles; traditional leaders teach respect for rules; praise and sanctions show which behaviour is accepted

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Elders and neighbours watch over children, correct them and give advice, so young people learn that good behaviour is expected everywhere and not only at home. At work parties (nhimbe / ilima) and community clean-ups, young people work with adults and learn cooperation and hard work. Ceremonies such as weddings and funerals also teach them customs and how to support others.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed point, one for a further relevant point.

explanation: Section A item on the agents of socialisation: definitions (a), matching agents (b) and explanation of the community's role (c).
hints: In (c), say what the community does and what young people learn from it.

stem: This question is about the media and ICT in socialisation.

parts.label: (a)

payload.template: Newspapers and magazines are {{blank:a}} media. Using phones or the internet to threaten or insult someone is called {{blank:b}}.

parts.explanation: Newspapers and magazines are print media; cyberbullying is bullying through ICT.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Match each example with the effect of ICT it shows.

left.content: A weekly video call with a parent working in another country
Watching revision videos before an examination
Forwarding a shocking message that has no source

parts.explanation: ICT can strengthen family ties and learning, but careless use spreads false information.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe ways in which young people can use the media and ICT responsibly.

points.description: Check the source, date and other reliable reports before believing or sharing a message, so false information is not spread
Keep personal information private and never meet online strangers, which protects them from fraud and abuse
Any one further way: limit screen time; choose age-appropriate content; report cyberbullying; think before posting (digital footprint)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Young people should check who made a message, when, and whether reliable sources report it before sharing it, so they do not spread false information. They should keep their address, location and passwords private and never meet online strangers, which protects them from fraud and abuse. They should also limit their screen time so they have time for study and family.

parts.explanation: Two marks per developed way, one for a further way.

explanation: Section A item on the media and ICT.
hints: In (c), think about checking information, privacy and time.

parts.label: (a)

payload.template: A totem is called mutupo in Shona and {{blank:a}} in Ndebele. In Shona and Ndebele custom, a child usually takes the totem of the {{blank:b}}.

parts.explanation: Mutupo / isibongo; children usually take their father's totem.

parts.label: (b)
parts.explanation: Shumba = lion; Dube = zebra; Nyathi = buffalo.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain the significance of the totem system.

points.description: People of the same totem are regarded as relatives, so the system prevents marriage between close relatives (incest)
Clan members do not kill or eat their totem animal, which helps to conserve it
Any one further point: gives identity and links a person to ancestors; unity and hospitality among clan members; respect through praises

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: People who share a totem are regarded as relatives descended from one ancestor, so the totem system prevents marriage between close relatives. Members of a clan do not kill or eat their totem animal, which helps to protect it. Totems also give people their identity, linking them to their clan and ancestors.

parts.explanation: Two marks per developed point, one for a further point.

hints: In (c), explain how each purpose works, not only name it.

stem: This question is about national identification documents.

parts.label: (a)

payload.template: Birth certificates, national identity cards and passports are issued by the {{blank:a}}. A national identity card is issued from the age of {{blank:b}}.

parts.explanation: The Registrar General issues all three documents; ID cards are issued from 16.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Match each document with a detail it records or a use it has.

right.content: Date of expiry for international travel
Needed to register as a voter

parts.explanation: Birth certificate: birth details and parents. ID card: identity inside Zimbabwe (voting, work). Passport: travel, with expiry date.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain the importance of national identification documents.

points.description: They prove identity and citizenship, so a person can register as a voter and vote
A birth certificate is needed to enrol at school and register for public examinations, so the right to education can be enjoyed
Any one further point: employment; travel (passport); banking or phone registration; proof of age protects children; government planning

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Identity documents prove who a person is and that they are a citizen, so an adult with an ID can register and vote. A birth certificate is needed to enrol at school and to register for public examinations, so a child can complete their education. A passport is also needed to travel to other countries.

parts.explanation: Two marks per developed point, one for a further point.

explanation: Section A item on national identification documents.
hints: In (c), link each document to something a person can do with it.

stem: This question is about the family and the media as agents of socialisation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the role of the family in the socialisation of children.

points.description: Teaches the first language and basic manners, such as greeting elders, so the child can communicate and live with others
Parents provide, protect and discipline, using rewards and sanctions to teach right and wrong
Grandparents, vatete / ubabakazi and sekuru / umalume pass on folk tales, totems, customs and advice on growing up
Children learn work and responsibility by taking part in household and farm tasks and caring for siblings

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The family is the first agent of socialisation. Parents and carers teach the child its first language and basic manners, such as greeting elders properly, so that the child can communicate and live with others.

Parents provide for and protect their children and discipline them, praising good behaviour and correcting bad behaviour, so children learn right from wrong.

The extended family also plays a part. Grandparents tell folk tales and teach the family's totem and praises, while the paternal aunt (vatete or ubabakazi) and maternal uncle (sekuru or umalume) advise young people on growing up and good conduct.

Finally, children learn work and responsibility by doing chores, helping in the fields or with animals, and caring for younger brothers and sisters.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed point (about four points).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "The media now play a greater role than the family in socialising young people in Zimbabwe." Discuss.

points.description: For: television, radio, phones and social media reach young people for many hours a day and supply role models, fashions and values
For: media and ICT influence spreads where parents work away or families spend less time together; advertising shapes wants
Against: the family comes first and shapes language, values, identity and totem; parents control and filter media use; many rural young people have limited access
Supported judgement weighing both sides (e.g. the media's influence has grown, but the family remains the foundation and decides how the media are used)

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The media have become a very powerful agent of socialisation. Many young people spend hours each day on phones, social media, television and radio. Musicians, athletes and online personalities become role models whose dress, speech and attitudes are copied, and advertising shapes what young people want. Where parents work far away or family members spend little time together, the media fill much of a young person's day.

However, the family remains extremely important. It is the first agent of socialisation, teaching language, manners, values, the totem and the sense of who a person is, and these early lessons usually last for life. Parents and guardians can set rules about screen time and content, discuss what children watch, and pass on heritage that the media do not provide. In many rural areas access to the internet and television is still limited, so the family and community remain the main influences.

The two agents also interact. A strong family can use the media positively, for example through video calls with distant relatives or educational programmes, while a weak family may leave young people to be shaped mostly by what they see online.

In conclusion, the media's influence has grown greatly, especially among teenagers in towns, but it has not replaced the family. The family remains the foundation of socialisation and largely decides whether the media's role is helpful or harmful, so the statement is only partly true.

parts.explanation: Level 4 (10-12): both sides developed with examples and a supported judgement.

explanation: Section B essay comparing the family and the media as agents of socialisation.
hints: In (b), consider how the answer differs for young children and teenagers, and for towns and rural areas.

stem: This question is about ICT and indigenous values.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the positive effects of ICT on the socialisation of young people.

points.description: Access to information and learning: revision videos and online lessons, for example during school closures
Communication: video and voice calls keep families separated by work or migration in touch, so guidance continues
Enterprise and skills: digital skills, mobile money and online selling prepare young people for work
Heritage and participation: folk tales, music and history shared in indigenous languages; joining community discussions and projects

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
ICT gives young people access to information and learning. They can watch revision videos, research topics and attend online lessons, as many did when schools closed during the COVID-19 pandemic.

It also keeps families together across distance. Parents working in other towns or countries use voice and video calls to guide their children and stay close.

ICT teaches useful skills: young people learn to use computers, mobile money and online selling, which prepares them for work and enterprise.

Finally, ICT can spread heritage and encourage participation. Elders' stories, praise poetry and music in indigenous languages are recorded and shared, and young people join discussions and organise community projects online.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed point.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far does ICT threaten indigenous values in Zimbabwe?

points.description: Threat: foreign trends and content that clash with unhu / ubuntu (e.g. disrespect for elders) reach young people directly
Threat: time online replaces time with elders, storytelling and indigenous languages; harmful content and cyberbullying undermine respect
Not a threat / benefit: ICT records and spreads folk tales, praises, music and languages; keeps families in touch; values depend on guidance and use
Supported judgement on 'how far'

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
ICT does pose a threat to indigenous values. Through phones and social media, young people meet foreign fashions, music and attitudes, some of which clash with unhu/ubuntu, for example content that treats disrespect for elders as funny. Time spent online often replaces evenings with grandparents, where folk tales, proverbs and family history were passed on, and many group chats use English or slang rather than indigenous languages. Cyberbullying and harmful content also undermine values such as respect and kindness.

However, ICT is not only a threat. It can preserve and spread indigenous values. Elders record voice notes of totem praises and family history, musicians and storytellers share work in Shona, Ndebele, Tonga and other languages, and community radio and online programmes teach culture to young people who live far from their home areas. Video calls let parents and grandparents continue guiding children. Foreign does not automatically mean bad, and young people can learn useful values online too.

Whether ICT threatens indigenous values depends largely on how it is used. Where families set rules, discuss content and use ICT to share heritage, it can strengthen values; where young people are left alone online for long hours, the threat is greater.

In conclusion, ICT threatens indigenous values to a considerable extent when it is used without guidance, but it is also one of the best tools for preserving them. The threat is real but not unavoidable.

parts.explanation: Level 4 (10-12): weighs threats against benefits with examples and reaches a supported judgement on 'how far'.

explanation: Section B essay on ICT and indigenous values.
hints: In (b), remember that 'foreign' is not the same as 'bad'; judge how far, not just whether.

stem: This question is about language, totems and identity.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain how language expresses a person's identity.

points.description: Names carry meaning in an indigenous language (e.g. Rudo, Sipho), linking a child to the family's language and history
Greetings and respectful forms of address show upbringing and membership of a community
Songs, folk tales, proverbs and praise poetry in the language pass on the community's heritage and values
A shared language creates belonging at community and national level; the 16 recognised languages show every group belongs

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Names are one of the clearest ways language expresses identity. Many Zimbabwean names, such as Rudo (love) or Sipho (gift), carry meaning in an indigenous language and link a child to the family's language and history.

Greetings also show identity. The way a person greets elders, with words such as mangwanani or salibonani and respectful gestures, shows their upbringing and community.

Songs, folk tales, proverbs and totem praises are passed on in the language, carrying the community's values and heritage.

Finally, sharing a language creates a sense of belonging. People who speak the same language often treat one another like relatives, and the Constitution's recognition of 16 languages shows that speakers of every language belong to the nation.

parts.explanation: Two marks for each developed point.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "Totems are more important than language in shaping a Zimbabwean's identity today." How far do you agree?

points.description: Totems: identify clan and ancestry; checked before marriage; used in thanks, praises and surnames; link to ancestors
Language: used every day; carries names, greetings, songs, values and heritage; links to community and nation; many people know their language better than their totem
Change today: many urban young people know little of their totem and some lose their indigenous language; both weakened in different ways
Supported judgement (e.g. the two work together; language is broader, totems more specific)

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Totems remain important in shaping identity. A totem tells a person which clan they belong to and links them to their ancestors. Families still ask about totems before marriage to avoid unions between relatives, people thank and honour one another with totem praises, and many surnames, such as Moyo, Ndlovu and Dube, are totem names. For many Zimbabweans, knowing their totem is knowing where they come from.

However, language shapes identity more widely and more constantly. People use their language every day, in their names, greetings, songs, prayers and jokes. It carries folk tales, proverbs and the values of unhu/ubuntu, and it links a person to their community and, through the 16 officially recognised languages, to the nation. Many young people know their home language well but know little about their totem or its praises.

Both forms of identity are changing. In towns some young people grow up speaking mainly English, while others do not know their totems. The two are also connected: totem praises are recited in an indigenous language, so losing the language weakens the totem tradition too.

Overall, I only partly agree. Totems are vital for clan identity and for decisions such as marriage, but language shapes identity in more areas of daily life and carries the totem tradition itself. Language is therefore the broader influence, while totems give a more specific sense of belonging.

parts.explanation: Level 4 (10-12): compares totems and language with examples and reaches a supported judgement.

explanation: Section B essay on language and totems in identity.
hints: In (b), compare how often and in how many areas of life each one shapes identity.
